title: Hadwiger's true constant
W: Among graphs whose chromatic number is at least t, what is the largest complete-graph minor they are all guaranteed to contain, as a fraction of t, when t is large? Hadwiger's conjecture says the fraction is 1. It is not even known to be bounded away from 0.
M: Let $h(G)$ be the Hadwiger number (largest $s$ with $K_s\preceq G$). Determine $c^*=\liminf_{t\to\infty}\ \inf\{h(G)/t:\ \chi(G)\ge t\}$. Trivially $c^*\le 1$, and Hadwiger's conjecture gives $c^*=1$. The known bound $\chi=O(t\log\log\log t)$ on $K_t$-minor-free graphs still only gives $c^*\ge 0$. In particular, is $c^*>0$?
why: This is the linear (asymptotic) form of Hadwiger's conjecture, one of the central problems in graph theory. The question c*>0 is the well-known Linear Hadwiger Conjecture.
diagnosis: Restates the Linear Hadwiger Conjecture (c*>0) and the asymptotic Hadwiger conjecture (c*=1). Famous, not novel; every natural variant (odd minors, fractional) is also already studied.
what_changed: Nothing. It cannot be upgraded honestly; drop it unless the list has a classic-problems section.

title: Spikes at the primes
W: Put a bump of fixed height at every prime on the half-line lattice and study the electron (discrete Schrodinger operator). What kind of spectrum does it have inside the free band (-2,2)? If the primes behaved like a random sparse set (Cramer model), the states would be localized (pure point spectrum); is that true for the actual primes?
M: Let $(Hu)(n)=u(n+1)+u(n-1)+\lambda\mathbf 1_{\mathbb P}(n)u(n)$ on $\ell^2(\mathbb N)$ with Dirichlet condition $u(0)=0$, $\lambda\ne0$. Determine the spectral type of $H$ on $(-2,2)$. In particular: is the spectral measure restricted to $(-2,2)$ pure point (with exponentially or sub-exponentially decaying eigenfunctions), or does it have a singular continuous part, e.g. near $E=0$?
why: It is the cleanest deterministic test of whether the primes are 'pseudo-random' for spectral theory: the random sparse model with site density 1/log n localizes, while deterministic sparse potentials typically produce singular continuous spectrum. The answer must use arithmetic input (distribution of primes in residue classes and gaps), linking Schrodinger operators to analytic number theory.
diagnosis: Has been posed numerically (cond-mat/0103313), and Bourgain's 'Moebius Schrodinger' (arXiv:1012.5217) studies the twin Mobius-potential question, leaving localization open. Low novelty, and the spectral-type question is hard to make decisive.
what_changed: No upgrade. Added Bourgain's Mobius analogue as context. Prime-potential numerics suggest delocalization near E=0, so the original pure-point framing was not reinstated.

title: Square-sum cliques
W: How many distinct positive integers can have every pairwise sum a perfect square? Five are known (Nicolas 1971); six is unknown. Decide whether the size is bounded.
M: Let $s=\sup\{|X|: X\subset\mathbb Z_{>0}\text{ finite},\ a+b\in\{k^2\}\ \forall a\ne b\in X\}$. Decide whether $s<\infty$ (the first open case: does a 6-element set exist?).
why: A classical Diophantine problem in the line of Diophantine m-tuples. The k-element sets are integral points on varieties that become of general type as k grows, so conjectures of Bombieri-Lang type predict a bound, but no unconditional bound is known.
diagnosis: Old, well-known open problem (Thatcher 1978; Prime Puzzles 70). The bound under Bombieri-Lang is also folklore. Valuable but not novel.
what_changed: Nothing; keep it only on a labelled classic list.

title: Monochromatic square-sum triangles, many colours
W: Colour the positive integers with finitely many colours. Show there are always three different numbers of the same colour whose three pairwise sums are all perfect squares.
M: Prove that for every $r\ge1$ and every colouring $\chi:\mathbb N\to\{1,\dots,r\}$ there exist distinct $a,b,c\in\mathbb N$ with $\chi(a)=\chi(b)=\chi(c)$ and $a+b,\ a+c,\ b+c$ all perfect squares. (Equivalently: the triangle hypergraph of the graph on $\mathbb N$ with $a\sim b\iff a+b=\square$ has infinite chromatic number.)
why: Khalfalah and Szemeredi proved that every finite colouring has a monochromatic pair x != y with x+y a square; this asks for the next configuration, a monochromatic triangle in the 'square-sum graph'. Density arguments fail (residue classes such as n = 1 mod 3 contain no such triangle), so a proof must be genuinely Ramsey-theoretic, in the same family as the open Pythagorean-triple and {x,y,x+y,xy} problems.
diagnosis: Natural next step after Khalfalah-Szemeredi, but a single specialised configuration. The general family (monochromatic k-cliques of the square-sum graph) stalls because 6-cliques are not known to exist at all.
what_changed: No upgrade. A search found no prior statement (partition-regularity literature on x+y=z^2, Pythagorean pairs, Rado over squares), so it stays a solid B.

title: Proof complexity of the sensitivity theorem
W: Huang proved that any set of more than half the corners of the n-cube contains a corner with at least √n neighbours inside the set. Write this as a propositional formula with one variable per corner. Do polynomial-size proofs exist in resolution, cutting planes or sum-of-squares, measured against the 2^n variables?
M: Let $N=2^n$, $d=\lceil\sqrt n\rceil-1$. $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ is the CNF on variables $x_v$ ($v\in\{0,1\}^n$) plus sequential-counter variables encoding $\sum_v x_v\ge 2^{n-1}+1$, together with the clauses $\neg x_v\vee\bigvee_{u\in U}\neg x_u$ for every $v$ and every $(d+1)$-set $U$ of neighbours of $v$ (size $N\cdot n^{O(\sqrt n)}=N^{1+o(1)}$). It is unsatisfiable by Huang's theorem. Does $\mathrm{SENS}_n$ have refutations of size $N^{O(1)}$ in (a) resolution, (b) cutting planes, (c) sum-of-squares of degree $O(\log N)$? Lower bounds $2^{N^{\Omega(1)}}$ are equally of interest.
why: Huang's proof is a short spectral argument, interlacing for a signed adjacency matrix. Asking whether weak proof systems can capture it tests how much linear algebra cutting planes and SOS can simulate. It belongs to the programme of locating famous combinatorial theorems in the proof-complexity hierarchy.
diagnosis: A niche instance in the programme of placing theorems in the proof-complexity hierarchy. Resolution is likely hard for routine matching reasons. Extended Frege likely has short proofs, since the argument is dimension counting on an eigenspace. Only cutting planes and SOS remain uncertain.
what_changed: No upgrade. Recommend rewording W around (b) cutting planes and (c) SOS. Searches found no prior work.

title: Ringel for forests
W: Ringel's conjecture, now a theorem for large n, says the complete graph on 2m+1 vertices splits into 2m+1 copies of any tree with m edges. Show the same holds for every forest with m edges. A stronger form asks that every such forest have a rho-labelling, which gives a cyclic decomposition.
M: Prove that for every $m\ge1$ and every forest $F$ with $m$ edges, $E(K_{2m+1})$ can be partitioned into $2m+1$ subgraphs each isomorphic to $F$. Stronger form: every such $F$ admits an injective map $f:V(F)\to\mathbb Z_{2m+1}$ whose edge lengths $\min(|f(u)-f(v)|,\,2m+1-|f(u)-f(v)|)$ are exactly $1,\dots,m$ (a $\rho$-labelling).
why: Montgomery-Pokrovskiy-Sudakov and Keevash-Staden proved Ringel's conjecture for large trees. Their rainbow-copy and cyclic-shift framework does not need connectivity, but the embedding steps do. So the question is whether connectivity is essential to Ringel-type decompositions. A positive answer would be a natural forest analogue of the Kotzig-Ringel-Rosa theorem.
diagnosis: A natural extension of a celebrated theorem and apparently not stated in the literature (MPS concluding remarks and Keevash-Staden cover trees only). But a large-m proof is plausibly an adaptation of the rainbow-embedding machinery, which caps the interest.
what_changed: No upgrade. Checked the MPS concluding remarks and the Kotzig-conjecture forest work: K_{2n+1} decomposes into rho-labelled forests (EJGTA), but that is not this statement.

title: Singularities of the permanental hypersurface
W: The hypersurface where the n x n determinant vanishes has rational singularities, the mildest kind that matters for much of its geometry. Decide whether the hypersurface where the n x n permanent vanishes has rational singularities for every n, and compute its minimal exponent, a finer measure of how mild a singularity is.
M: Let $X_n=\{\operatorname{per}_n=0\}\subset\mathbb A^{n^2}_{\mathbb C}$ and let $\tilde\alpha(X_n)$ be Saito's minimal exponent (the smallest root of $b_{\operatorname{per}_n}(-s)/(1-s)$), so that $\operatorname{lct}(\mathbb A^{n^2},X_n)=\min\{1,\tilde\alpha(X_n)\}$ and $X_n$ has rational singularities iff $\tilde\alpha(X_n)>1$. For $n=2$, $X_2$ is a nondegenerate quadric cone in $\mathbb A^4$ and $\tilde\alpha=2$. For $\det_n$ the Bernstein--Sato polynomial is $\prod_{i=1}^n(s+i)$, so $\tilde\alpha(\{\det_n=0\})=2$ for all $n$. Determine $\tilde\alpha(X_n)$ for all $n\ge3$ (in particular for $n=3$), and decide whether $X_n$ has rational singularities for every $n$. Note: restricting to a generic linear subspace of dimension $r=\operatorname{codim}\operatorname{Sing}(X_n)$ gives an isolated homogeneous singularity, so $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\ge r/n$. Since $6\le r\le 2n$ is known and $r=2n$ is conjectured, that conjecture would give $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\ge2$ and rational singularities. Sharpened question: is $\tilde\alpha(X_n)=2$ for all $n$, or does $\tilde\alpha(X_n)\to\infty$?
why: Determinantal varieties are the model case of a well-understood singular variety; permanental varieties, which are central in algebraic complexity (Valiant's VP vs VNP, geometric complexity theory), have almost no geometric results. The minimal exponent is a single number that would quantify how differently the two polynomials behave geometrically.
diagnosis: Narrow. It is also tied to a known conjecture: restricting to a generic linear subspace of dimension r = codim Sing gives an isolated homogeneous singularity, so minimal exponent >= r/n. Known r in [6,2n], so codim=2n would give >= 2, hence rational singularities.
what_changed: Added the bound: minimal exponent(per_n) >= codim(Sing per_n)/n. The conjectured codim 2n (2402.17839, Conj. 4.27) implies rationality, so the rationality part is close to a known conjecture. What remains is the exact value (is it 2, as for det, or does it grow?). The n=3 case is for computer algebra.

title: First-order convergence law for random Latin squares
W: Pick a Latin square of order n uniformly at random and read it as a multiplication table x∘y on n symbols. Does every first-order statement about this table have a limiting probability as n grows? A zero-one law fails: the number of x with x∘x=x should be asymptotically Poisson(1), so the probability that one exists should tend to 1−1/e rather than 0 or 1.
M: Let $L_n$ be uniform among Latin squares on $[n]$ and $\mathcal Q_n=([n],\circ)$ with $x\circ y=L_n(x,y)$. Prove or disprove: for every first-order sentence $\varphi$ in the language $\{\circ,=\}$, $\lim_{n\to\infty}\Pr[\mathcal Q_n\models\varphi]$ exists. Expected route: (i) an extension property, under which every finite partial-quasigroup configuration extends in every consistent way w.h.p.; (ii) a joint Poisson limit for the counts of all sparse definable configurations with bounded expectation, such as cycles of the diagonal map $x\mapsto x\circ x$, as for Lynch's random unary functions. A disproof would need a definable sparse statistic with no limit law.
why: Convergence laws are known for G(n,p), sparse random graphs, random functions and permutations, all of which have independence or exchangeable structure. A uniform Latin square is the canonical dense random algebraic object with rigid global constraints, where such tools fail. New 'independent model' approximations (Kwan-Sah-Sawhney-Simkin; Parities in random Latin squares, 2509.13125, resolving Cameron's conjecture) make it timely. The answer would say what first-order logic can see of a random quasigroup.
diagnosis: Marked B mainly because the literature check was incomplete. The question itself is natural (the canonical random dense algebraic structure), decisive (a convergence law, yes or no), not found posed, and hard. Recent independent-model approximations make it timely.
what_changed: Searches found no FO-law work on Latin squares or quasigroups. Sharpened it into a decisive convergence-law question and named the expected mechanism: an extension property plus a Poisson limit for sparse definable configurations.

title: Distinct character degrees of the symmetric group
W: Conjugate partitions always give representations of S_n of the same dimension, so at most about half of the p(n) irreducible representations can have distinct dimensions. Decide whether the fraction of distinct dimensions tends to a limit, and whether that limit is positive.
M: Let $d(n)=\#\{f^\lambda:\lambda\vdash n\}$ be the number of distinct irreducible character degrees of $S_n$, so $d(n)\le (p(n)+sc(n))/2$, where $sc(n)$ is the number of self-conjugate partitions. Determine whether $\lim_{n\to\infty}d(n)/p(n)$ exists and, if so, find it; in particular decide whether $\liminf_n d(n)/p(n)>0$. (Hook-length data: $d(n)/p(n)\in[0.40,0.47]$ for $20\le n\le45$, e.g. $d(40)=16216$, $p(40)=37338$; computations up to $n=129$ in arXiv:2410.01726 show the average multiplicity $p(n)/d(n)$ with no clear limit, possibly near $2.5$.)
why: Degrees of S_n are products of hook lengths, and coincidences between them beyond conjugation are a basic but poorly understood arithmetic phenomenon. Whether the average degree multiplicity stays bounded says how much of the information in a partition is lost in its dimension.
diagnosis: Already posed in essence by arXiv:2410.01726, which asks whether p(n)/|cd(S_n)| has a limit (a referee suggested pi*sqrt(2/3)). Open but not novel; a borderline drop.
what_changed: No upgrade possible; the natural sharpening (liminf>0) is the paper's own question.

title: Blank jigsaw with few edge shapes
W: A jigsaw with no picture can only be solved from the shapes of its pieces. Each internal edge is one of k shapes (a tab that fits only its own matching blank), and pieces may be turned. How small can k be if some n×n blank jigsaw still goes together in exactly one way? Counting shows k must be at least about √n, and random puzzles need about n.
M: An $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types is a map assigning to each internal edge of the $n\times n$ grid a type in $[k]$ and an orientation (which side carries the tab); border edges are flat. Its pieces are the $n^2$ unit squares, each regarded as a distinct physical object carrying its four (type, tab/blank) labels up to rotation. An assembly is a placement of all pieces bijectively on the cells, each rotated by a multiple of $90^\circ$, so that every internal edge joins a tab and a blank of the same type and all flat edges lie on the border. Let $k(n)$ be the least $k$ for which some $n\times n$ jigsaw with $k$ edge types has exactly one assembly up to the four rotations of the whole square. Determine the order of $k(n)$; in particular, is $k(n)=\Theta(\sqrt n)$?
why: Uniqueness of jigsaw reconstruction is a well-studied model problem for shotgun assembly (Mossel–Ross; Bordenave–Feige–Mossel; Nenadov–Pfister–Steger), but all known thresholds concern random puzzles, where about n edge types are needed. Since unique assembly forces all n^2 pieces to be distinct, a simple count gives k(n) ≥ c√n, so the question is whether designed puzzles can beat random ones by a polynomial factor, a rigidity/design question in the spirit of de Bruijn tori.
diagnosis: Pleasant and well defined, but narrow. The only content is Theta(sqrt n) versus larger, and an explicit coordinate-encoding design might settle it routinely. The unlabelled variant is closer to self-assembly tile-complexity results.
what_changed: No upgrade. The ambiguity was already fixed (distinct physical pieces).
